comments.text_zh: 另外，我觉得这些也很有意思：The Unix-Haters Handbook（1994）包含很多历史，能把你带回过去……[LINK] Brian Kernighan“采访”Ken Thompson（2019）——Ken 讲故事。他们俩都非常有趣，这个视频非常好看，有些故事我（甚至 Brian）都没听过。[VIDEO] UNIX: Making Computers Easier To Use（1982）[LINK] 还有，前几天我在 AWK 书里读到，它主要受 SNOBOL4 启发，所以我在 archive.org 上看了一些 1970 到 1972 年以及稍早一点的 SNOBOL4 书，比 Unix 历史能带你回溯的年代还稍早一些。其中一本讲如何组织你的打孔卡来输入程序……另一本有一个参考文献目录，列了几十本 SNOBOL 书。显然它被人文学科的人广泛使用；和 AWK 一样，它处理文字和文本很拿手。
comments.text: Also I found these fascinating: The Unix-Haters Handbook (1994) has a lot of history and takes you back in time.. [LINK] Brian Kernighan 'interviews' Ken Thompson (2019) - Ken telling stories. They're both very funny, a very entertaining video, some stories I (and even Brian) hadn't heard. [VIDEO] UNIX: Making Computers Easier To Use (1982) [LINK] Also the other day I read in the AWK book that it was mainly inspired by SNOBOL4, so looked at some SNOBOL4 books from archive.org, from 1970-2 and just before, slightly earlier than Unix history takes you back. One tells you how to organize your punch cards to feed in the program.. Another had a bibliography with many dozens of SNOBOL books. It was widely used by people in the humanities apparently; like AWK it was at home dealing with words and text.

comments.author: dwcnnnghm
comments.story_title: The Birth of Unix with Brian Kernighan
comments.why_zh: Ken 描述了 McIlroy 了不起的 TMG 自我编译以及 B 的起源
comments.quote_zh: 在与 Brian Kernighan 一场非常有趣的、关于 Unix 历史的对话中
comments.text_zh:
> Brian 超级谦虚，声称自己是个糟糕的程序员，但他是在拿自己和 Ken Thompson 比，而他认为 Ken 简直不可思议。Ken 曾经为一台小型计算机写了一个反汇编器、汇编器和 B 解释器；那台小型计算机驱动着一台他们一直搞不定的打印机，他花几天时间写好，让他们能重新打印。这让 Brian 大为震撼。再往上一个层次，这里是 Ken（在与 Brian Kernighan 一场非常有趣的、关于 Unix 历史的对话中）描述 McIlroy：

> McIlroy 不断被提到。他是我们所有人中最聪明的，也是最不被记住（或被记录下来）的……McIlroy 坐在那儿，在一张纸上——注意，不是在计算机上——写下了用 TMG 写的 TMG [一个专有的、类似 yacc 的程序]……然后！他现在有了用 TMG 写的 TMG，他决定把自己的那张纸交给自己的那张纸，并写下出来的东西（代码）。他确实这么做了。然后他走到我的编辑器旁，把他的代码输入进去，汇编它，而且（我不会说没有错误，但错误少得让你吃惊）他在 PDP-7 上搞出了一个用 TMG 写的 TMG 编译器。这是我一生中见过的最基础、最精简、最令人印象深刻的自我编译。顺便说一下，这个故事引出了 Ken 如何创造 B（以及它最终如何被 Dennis Ritchie 改进成 C）。[0] [VIDEO]
comments.text: > Brian is super modest and claims to be a horrible programmer but he is comparing himself to Ken Thompson, who he thinks is just incredible. Ken once wrote a disassembler, assembler and B interpreter for a mini-computer that ran a printer they were struggling with, in a couple of days, so that they could get it printing again. This blew Brian's mind. For the next level up here's Ken (in a very interesting conversation with Brian Kernighan about the history of Unix) describing McIlroy: > McIlroy keeps coming up. He's the smartest of all of us and the least remembered (or written down)... McIlroy sat there and wrote ---on a piece of paper, now, not on a computer--- TMG [a proprietary yacc-like program] written in TMG... And then! He now has TMG written in TMG, he decided to give his piece of paper to his piece of paper and write down what came out (the code). Which he did. And then he came over to my editor and he typed in his code, assembled it, and (I won't say without error, but with so few errors you'd be astonished) he came up with a TMG compiler, on the PDP-7, written in TMG. And it's the most basic, bare, impressive self-compilation I've ever seen in my life. This story, by the way, leads into how Ken created B (and how that was eventually improved by Dennis Ritchie into C). [0] [VIDEO]

comments.text: The article provides ancillary hyperlinks to nearly every topic mentioned, but fails to link the actual video of Kernighan speaking. Here it is: [LINK] In reality the subject of the talk is Kernighan’s perspective of the history of Unix at Bell Labs. The questions covered in the article are the least interesting part, and make up about six minutes at the very end—a small fraction not just of the 70-minute video, but even of the 30-minute Q&A session. In short, the headline and article are disappointing clickbait, but the video itself is worth watching for Kernighan’s relating of history and his theories about what confluence of factors made Unix successful (collegial environment, good management, overall mission…). comments.author: ghoward
comments.story_title: Lorinda Cherry, author of dc, bc, eqn has died
comments.text_zh: 作为少数几个实现过 `dc` 和 `bc` 的作者之一，但也是从未真正见过 Lorinda Cherry 本人的人，也许我对她的工作有略微不同的看法。我读过我们能找到的最接近 `dc` 和 `bc` 原始源码的东西：Plan 9 随附的源码。我没花多久就读完了全部源码，因为它们简单而简洁。这让我印象极深。然而，我很不想说，我的年轻（至少相对于 Cherry 女士而言）让我当初带着轻蔑的眼光看这份源码，主要是因为它没有处理用户失误造成的错误。我花了几天时间才更仔细地思考当时的背景。她是在为自己和其他程序员写代码，他们大概能认出自己什么时候犯了错并修正。这份代码有一种我的代码永远不会有的简洁优雅。当然，你或许会说我的代码是“工业级强度”，但我觉得 ** Gabriel 的一句话很好地概括了 Cherry 女士的代码和我的代码之间的区别：“早期编程语言那种轻巧与静谧总让我感到愉悦。文字不多；却能完成很多事。旧程序读起来像一位谈吐得体的研究工作者和一位训练有素的机械同事之间的安静对话，而不是与编译器的一场辩论。谁能想到，精巧复杂竟带来了这样的噪音？”[1] 而这还完全没说到她软件的设计。`dc` 曾经是，而且在很多方面现在仍然是，可能存在过的最简单的计算器。它也是最简单的 shell，凭借 `!` com
comments.text: As one of few authors of an implementation of `dc` and `bc`, but one who never actually met Lorinda Cherry, perhaps I have a slightly different perspective of her work. I've read the closest thing we have to the original sources of `dc` and `bc`: the source bundled with Plan 9. It didn't take me long to read the entirety of the source because they were simple and concise. That immensely impressed me. However, I hate to say that my youth (compared to Ms. Cherry, at least) caused me to look at the source with disdain, mostly from a lack of handling errors caused by user mistakes. It took several days for me to think more carefully about the context. She was writing for herself and other programmers, who would probably be able to recognize when they made a mistake and fix it. The code has a simple elegance that mine will never have. Sure, you might call mine "industrial strength," but I think a quote by ** Gabriel sums up the difference between Ms. Cherry's code and mine: "I'm always delighted by the light touch and stillness of early programming languages. Not much text; a lot gets done. Old programs read like quiet conversations between a well-spoken research worker and a well-studied mechanical colleague, not as a debate with a compiler. Who'd have guessed sophistication bought such noise?" [1] And that says nothing of the design of her software. `dc` was, and in many ways still is, the simplest calculator that could ever exist. comments.quote_zh: 聊着聊着就说到管道，dc 在那里又出现了一次
comments.text_zh: 我好奇的问题是：“为什么 POSIX 要求一元负号具有更高的优先级？”是因为“70 年代 bc 就是这么工作的，因为这样写解析器更容易”？还是有某种更深层的原因——“如果一元负号的优先级低于二元运算符，这个问题就会变得非常棘手，还会让其他表达式变得不那么合理”？这有点像逻辑 XOR 的问题（[链接]）……而我认为这个设计选择背后是有实实在在的理由的。（题外话：另一个关于“事情为什么是这样的”的历史话题，涉及 dc 在历史上的地位：Brian Kernighan 在 VCF East 2019 上采访 Ken Thompson [视频]——聊着聊着就说到管道，dc 在那里又出现了一次）
comments.text: The question that I'm curious about is "why does POSIX require unary negation to have a higher precedence?" Was it a "this is the way that bc worked in the 70s because it was easier to write a parser for it?" or was there some more underlying reason for the "this problem gets really icky if unary negation has lower precedence than the binary operators and makes for other expressions that become less reasonable?" It's like the Logical XOR issue ( [LINK] ) ... and I'm of the opinion that there's a real reason why this design choice was made. (Aside: Some other historical "why things work that way" touching on dc's place in history: Ken Thompson interviewed by Brian Kernighan at VCF East 2019 [VIDEO] - it goes on to pipes and dc makes an appearance there again)
